target_audience: University Freshmen and AP Calculus Students

sections.title: Introduction: Explicit vs. Implicit
sections.content: Introduce the concept by comparing 'Explicit' functions (where y is isolated, like a clear path) and 'Implicit' relations (where x and y are tangled together). Explain that we need implicit differentiation when solving for y is difficult or impossible.
sections.example: Visual: A 'Function Robot' neatly outputting y from x (Explicit: y = x^2) vs. two characters, 'X-Bot' and 'Y-Bot', tied together in a knot (Implicit: x² + y² = 25).

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Chain Rule Reminder
sections.content: Review the Chain Rule, as it is the engine of implicit differentiation. Emphasize that whenever we differentiate a term involving 'y', we must treat y as a function of x, meaning we multiply by dy/dx (y').
sections.example: Animation: Show d/dx [f(x)³] = 3[f(x)]² · f'(x). Then, replace f(x) with 'y' to show d/dx [y³] = 3y² · dy/dx.

sections.title: The Golden Rule: Differentiate Both Sides
sections.content: Teach the core procedural step: Apply the derivative operator (d/dx) to every single term on both sides of the equation. Use a balance scale visual to show that the equality remains as long as we treat both sides equally.
sections.example: Mathematical Step: For x² + y² = 25, apply d/dx to the left and d/dx to the right. Result: 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0.

sections.title: The Algebraic Clean-up
sections.content: Guide the student through isolating dy/dx. This involves moving all terms with dy/dx to one side, factoring out dy/dx, and dividing. Emphasize that the result often contains both x and y.
sections.example: Step-by-step UI: 2y(dy/dx) = -2x → dy/dx = -2x / 2y → dy/dx = -x/y. Use color-coding to highlight the dy/dx term moving across the '=' sign.

sections.title: Visualizing the Slope on a Curve
sections.content: Use a graphical representation of the Unit Circle to show that the derivative we found (-x/y) represents the slope of the tangent line at any point (x, y), even though the circle isn't a single function.
sections.example: Graphical: Plot the point (3, 4) on a circle of radius 5. Plug values into dy/dx = -3/4. Show a 'Tangent Laser' rotating to that exact slope on the graph.

sections.title: Real-World Application: The Growing Bubble
sections.content: Conclude with a brief look at why this matters. Mention 'Related Rates' where variables change over time. Use an expanding soap bubble as a device to show how volume and radius are implicitly linked.
sections.example: Character: A 'Scientific Squirrel' blowing a bubble. As the radius (r) increases, the volume (V) changes. V = 4/3πr³. Differentiating both sides with respect to time (t) uses the same implicit logic.
